title: Abram and Sarai in Egypt (Genesis 12:10–20)
hookLine: famine, fear and a half-truth that nearly costs everything; the Torah doesn't hide its heroes' faults

cards: Abram has just arrived in the land God promised him, and the first thing that happens there is a famine. So he keeps going, south, down to Egypt, where there's grain. At the border, he turns to his wife.
You're beautiful, he tells Sarai. When the Egyptians see you, they'll kill me and keep you. Say you're my sister, so that it goes well with me because of you.
And that's exactly what happens. Pharaoh's officials see her, praise her to Pharaoh, and she's taken into the palace. Abram, the brother, is rewarded with sheep and cattle and donkeys and camels.
The man who was just promised a great name is standing in Egypt, getting rich, while his wife is in another man's house.

teach.h: WHAT IS THIS THOU HAST DONE?
teach.b: Then God strikes Pharaoh's household with plagues, and Pharaoh figures it out.
He calls Abram in, and in the old JPS translation he says: "What is this that thou hast done unto me? why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?" Think about who's asking.
Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is the one with the moral question. Abram doesn't answer. Pharaoh gives Sarai back and sends them away.
Was it a lie? Later in Genesis, in a very similar scene, Abraham says Sarah really is his half-sister, the daughter of his father but not his mother.
So, a half-truth, told to save himself, while she paid the price. The rabbis did not look away.
Nachmanides, the great thirteenth-century commentator, says it plainly: Abram sinned. He put his righteous wife at risk out of fear, and he should have trusted God to protect them both.
Others defend him: the danger was real, and he had no good choices. Jewish tradition keeps both voices in the room. And notice what the Torah never tells us: what Sarai said, or felt.
Her voice is silent here. Nachmanides also noticed a pattern. Famine sends a family down to Egypt; Pharaoh's house is struck with plagues; they leave with wealth.
That's the whole book of Exodus in a few verses.
The rabbis had a saying for it: what happens to the parents is a sign for the children.
The first hero stumbled, and the Torah wrote it down.

how: Jews read this episode in the Torah portion Lech Lecha, and commentaries such as Nachmanides are studied alongside it, including his criticism of Abram's choices.

s: the Torah hides the faults of its heroes
it tells Abram's fear and half-truth in full, and Pharaoh gets the moral question.
Sarah was, in a sense, Abraham's half-sister
later in Genesis he says she is his father's daughter, not his mother's.
the Torah tells us what Sarai said in Egypt
it's silent about her words and feelings.

games.q: you're Pharaoh. your house is struck with plagues, and you learn the woman you took is Abram's wife. what do you do?
o: give her back and send them away.
games.why: he asks, "what is this thou hast done unto me?" then returns Sarai and sends them off, with everything Abram gained.

practice: Look back over the last few days for one small untruth, the ordinary kind: I'm fine, I didn't see your message, I'm almost there. Notice what it protected, fear, comfort, someone's feelings, and who paid for it, even a little.
Don't punish yourself; just admit it to yourself, honestly, and if you pray, you can bring it into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Nachmanides, the thirteenth-century commentator who said plainly that Abram sinned, putting his wife at risk out of fear instead of trusting God to protect them both.

orig.note: Hebrew: my sister. Abram asks Sarai to call herself this at the border.

carryVoice: Your line: heroes stumble too. And the stumble isn't the end of his story. Day thirty-nine, done.
